hero.title: A little about me
hero.desc: Developer, tinkerer, lifelong learner — here's the short version.

who.heading: Who I am
who.p1: Hi, I'm Yang Guang — a developer who enjoys building things that live on the web. Whether it's a web app, a small CLI tool, or an AI experiment, if it involves code I'm probably curious about it.
who.p2: I come from a full-stack background. Over the years I've quietly shipped corporate sites, content platforms, and data products, often moving things forward through collaboration. What I really care about isn't just the code — it's how content flows, how ideas travel, and how AI can actually fit into the way teams work day to day.
who.p3: I started with curiosity and a text editor. That curiosity has slowly grown into a quiet appreciation for clean architecture, thoughtful design, and making technology feel a bit more human.

doing.heading: What I do
doing.p1: I build full-stack applications, explore AI tooling, and write down what I learn along the way. These days I'm focused on making complex ideas easier to understand — through small tools, clear writing, and honest examples.

site.heading: About this site
site.p1: This site is a static, hand-crafted portal — plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with no frameworks or build tools. It's meant to stay fast, light, and easy to host almost anywhere. The design language borrows from

hero.title: Access Control Models Explained
hero.desc: A comprehensive guide to ACL, RBAC, ABAC, PBAC, DAC, and MAC — covering core concepts, tradeoffs, analogies, and the right scenarios for each model.

intro.p1: Access control is at the heart of every secure system. Whether you're building a document collaboration tool, a multi-tenant SaaS platform, or a government-grade secure system, choosing the right access control model is a decision that will shape your architecture for years to come.
intro.p2: This guide walks through six mainstream models — ACL, RBAC, ABAC, PBAC, DAC, and MAC — explaining what each one does well, where it falls short, and when to use it.

acl.heading: 01 / ACL — Access Control List
acl.fullName: Access Control List · 访问控制列表
acl.title: The Whitelist Approach

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: Each resource carries an explicit list of who is allowed to access it. Think of it as a guest list taped to the door of a private event.

acl.analogy: A whitelist posted on a meeting room door — only listed individuals may enter.

cons.1: Fragmented, hard to manage at scale

acl.scenario: Document systems, collaboration platforms (Notion, Trello), any scenario where permissions are resource-specific.

rbac.heading: 02 / RBAC — Role-Based Access Control
rbac.fullName: Role-Based Access Control · 基于角色的访问控制
rbac.title: The Organizational Approach

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: Permissions are assigned to roles; users inherit permissions by being assigned a role. This is the model most enterprise systems grow into.

rbac.analogy: Employees gain access based on their job title — managers, staff, and guests each get a different set of keys.

pros.1: Clean structure, easy to reason about

rbac.scenario: Enterprise back-office systems, HR/ERP/CMS systems, any organization with stable role definitions.

abac.heading: 03 / ABAC — Attribute-Based Access Control
abac.fullName: Attribute-Based Access Control · 基于属性的访问控制
abac.title: The Context-Aware Approach

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: Access decisions are evaluated dynamically based on attributes of the user, the resource, and the environment. This enables fine-grained, context-sensitive authorization.

abac.analogy: Allow access if: department = Finance AND resource = Report AND time < 18:00.

cons.1: Complex to configure and reason about
cons.2: Policies can be hard to test and debug

abac.scenario: Multi-tenant SaaS platforms, conditional access systems, scenarios requiring dynamic, attribute-driven decisions.

pbac.heading: 04 / PBAC — Policy-Based Access Control
pbac.fullName: Policy-Based Access Control · 基于策略的访问控制
pbac.title: The Centralized Policy Approach

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: Access control is governed by centrally managed, reusable policy rules — often written in a dedicated policy language. This enables auditability and consistent enforcement across systems.

pbac.analogy: Like an organization's internal policy handbook — every action must be justified by a written rule.

pros.2: Integrates well with OPA, Casbin, and other policy engines

pbac.scenario: Zero-trust architectures, multi-tenant systems, compliance platforms — anywhere centralized policy governance is required.

dac.heading: 05 / DAC — Discretionary Access Control
dac.fullName: Discretionary Access Control · 自主访问控制
dac.title: The Owner-Driven Approach

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: The owner of a resource decides who can access it, at their own discretion. This is the model behind file permissions in operating systems and sharing features in collaboration tools.

dac.analogy: The file owner sets "who can open this file" — just like sharing a Google Doc with specific people.

pros.2: Flexible and easy to grant access

dac.scenario: File sharing systems, OS file permissions (Linux), any scenario where resource owners should control access.

mac.heading: 06 / MAC — Mandatory Access Control
mac.fullName: Mandatory Access Control · 强制访问控制
mac.title: The Security-First Approach

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: The system enforces access based on security labels assigned to both users and resources — users cannot override these rules. This is the model used in high-security environments.

mac.analogy: A "Top Secret" document can only be accessed by people with the matching clearance level — no exceptions.
mac.scenario: Military/government systems, financial core platforms — anywhere maximum security is the priority.

hybrid.heading: Hybrid Patterns: Mixing Models in Practice
hybrid.intro: In real-world engineering, no single model fits all requirements. The most effective systems layer multiple models to balance structure, flexibility, and security.
hybrid.pattern1: Role-based structure for most access, with fine-grained per-resource overrides via ACL. Common in document management and collaboration tools.
hybrid.pattern2: Roles define baseline permissions; attributes enforce dynamic, context-sensitive restrictions on top. Ideal for SaaS platforms with varying tenant rules.
hybrid.pattern3: Enterprise-grade combination for large platforms, zero-trust architectures, or multi-tenant systems requiring full auditability and policy governance.

decision.heading: How to Choose: A Decision Guide
decision.intro: Still not sure which model fits your system? Answer these questions to narrow it down:
decision.q1: Are your user roles stable and clearly defined across the system?
decision.q2: Do different resources need different access rules (per-file, per-record)?
decision.q3: Do you need dynamic, context-sensitive access (time, location, device)?
decision.q4: Do you need centralized, auditable policies for compliance or zero-trust?
decision.q5: Should individual resource owners control their own sharing and access?
decision.q6: Is the highest security priority — even at the cost of flexibility?

access-control-models.conclusion: Access control is never one-size-fits-all. The best systems start with a clear understanding of their security requirements, user workflows, and growth trajectory — then pick the model (or combination of models) that fits. If you're designing a new system, take the time to map out your access patterns before writing a single line of authorization code. Your future self will thank you.
